import cv2
import numpy as np
import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.rcParams['figure.figsize'] = (5, 3)     
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 120            
plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 8             
plt.rcParams['axes.titlesize'] = 9
plt.rcParams['axes.labelsize'] = 8
plt.rcParams['xtick.labelsize'] = 7
plt.rcParams['ytick.labelsize'] = 7
plt.rcParams['figure.autolayout'] = True   
def intensity_transform(im, breakpoints):
    x = breakpoints[:, 0]
    y = breakpoints[:, 1]
    lut = np.interp(np.arange(256), x, y)
    lut = np.clip(lut, 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)
    transformed_im = lut[im]
    return transformed_im
eps = 1e-5
breakpoints = np.array([
    [0,0],
    [50,50],
    [50,100],
    [150,255],
    [150,150],
    [255,255],
])
im1 = cv2.imread('Images/emma.jpg', cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
assert im1 is not None
intensity_transformed_im1 = intensity_transform(im1, breakpoints)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(7.5, 2.0))
axes[0].imshow(im1, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[0].set_title("Original Image")
axes[0].axis("off")
axes[1].imshow(intensity_transformed_im1, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[1].set_title("Transformed Image (Set 1)")
axes[1].axis("off")
axes[2].plot(breakpoints[:, 0], breakpoints[:, 1], "ro-", linewidth=2, markersize=5)
axes[2].set_xlim(0, 255)
axes[2].set_ylim(0, 255)
axes[2].set_xlabel("Input Intensity")
axes[2].set_ylabel("Output Intensity")
axes[2].set_title("Intensity Transformation (Given Breakpoints)")
axes[2].grid(True, linestyle="--", alpha=0.6)

The given transform has caused the middle range of pixels to have higher intensities, while keeping the highest range of pixels unchanged. In my tuned transform, I have adjusted the intensity transform to brighten the middle range of pixels without having any jumps, to keep the image looking visually pleasing.

The gamma correction has shifted and adjusted the histogram of the L channel to the right, which has brightened the image and made the white matter more visible. The gamma value of 0.6 was chosen after trial and error to find the most visually pleasing image. The gamma correction function has also amplified the noise already present in the L plane (visible in the original histogram), causing more significant noise spikes due to the non-linear nature of gamma correction function.

im5 = cv2.imread("Images/shells.tif", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
assert im5 is not None
def hist_equal(image):
    L = 256
    M, N = image.shape
    hist = cv2.calcHist([image], [0], None, [L], [0, L])
    cdf = np.cumsum(hist)
    transform_map = np.array([(L-1)/(M*N)*cdf[k] for k in range (256)]).astype("uint8")
    equalized_image = transform_map[image]
    return equalized_image
im5_equalized = hist_equal(im5)
hist_orig = cv2.calcHist([im5], [0], None, [256], [0, 256]).ravel()
hist_eq = cv2.calcHist([im5_equalized], [0], None, [256], [0, 256]).ravel()
bins = np.arange(256)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(6.5, 1.8))
axes[0].imshow(im5, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[0].set_title("Original Image")
axes[0].axis("off")
axes[1].bar(bins, hist_orig, width=1.0, color="black", edgecolor="none")
axes[1].set_title("Histogram Before Equalization")
axes[1].set_xlim([0, 256])
axes[1].set_xlabel("Pixel Value (8-bit)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Pixel Count")
axes[1].grid(alpha=0.3)
axes[2].imshow(im5_equalized, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=255)
axes[2].set_title("Equalized Image")
axes[2].axis("off")
axes[3].bar(bins, hist_eq, width=1.0, color="crimson", edgecolor="none")
axes[3].set_title("Histogram After Equalization")
axes[3].set_xlim([0, 256])
axes[3].set_xlabel("Pixel Value (8-bit)")
axes[3].set_ylabel("Pixel Count")
axes[3].grid(alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Histogram equalisation has enhanced the brightness of regions of the image by shifting a uniform distribution of the pixel intensities. This has also amplified the noise present in the image however, since noise is present in the entire range of intensities. There's also a loss of contrast in the image, since the pixel intensities have been shifted to a uniform distribution.

im6 = cv2.imread("Images/woman.jpeg")
assert im6 is not None

im6_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(im6, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
im6_hsv = cv2.cvtColor(im6, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
h_plane, s_plane, v_plane = cv2.split(im6_hsv)
_, mask = cv2.threshold(s_plane, 15, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
mask_inv = cv2.bitwise_not(mask)
hist_foreground = cv2.calcHist([v_plane], [0], mask, [256], [0, 256])
cumsum = np.cumsum(hist_foreground)
foreground_size = cumsum[-1]
L = 256
transform_map = np.array(((L - 1) / foreground_size) * cumsum).astype(np.uint8)
v_equalized = transform_map[v_plane]
v_foreground_new = cv2.bitwise_and(v_equalized, v_equalized, mask=mask)
v_background = cv2.bitwise_and(v_plane, v_plane, mask=mask_inv)
final_v = cv2.add(v_background, v_foreground_new)
final_hsv = cv2.merge([h_plane, s_plane, final_v])
final_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(final_hsv, cv2.COLOR_HSV2RGB)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(6.5, 3.0))
axes[0, 0].imshow(h_plane, cmap="gray")
axes[0, 0].set_title("Hue Plane")
axes[0, 0].axis("off")
axes[0, 1].imshow(s_plane, cmap="gray")
axes[0, 1].set_title("Saturation Plane")
axes[0, 1].axis("off")
axes[0, 2].imshow(v_plane, cmap="gray")
axes[0, 2].set_title("Value Plane")
axes[0, 2].axis("off")
axes[1, 0].imshow(mask, cmap="gray")
axes[1, 0].set_title("Foreground Mask")
axes[1, 0].axis("off")
axes[1, 1].imshow(im6_rgb)
axes[1, 1].set_title("Original Image")
axes[1, 1].axis("off")
axes[1, 2].imshow(final_rgb)
axes[1, 2].set_title("Result with Equalized Foreground")
axes[1, 2].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

I selected the saturation plane as the ideal one for foreground mask since it contains most of the intensity values needed from the foreground subject. After extracting the mask, I applied histogram equalisation on the Value plane, to ensure that only the brightness values are equalised across the foreground (instead of equalising the color intensities and distorting the image).

im7 = cv2.imread("Images/einstein.jpeg", cv2.IMREAD_GRAYSCALE)
assert im7 is not None

sobel = np.array([[1,0,-1], [2, 0, -2], [1, 0, -1]], dtype=np.float32)
filtered1 = cv2.filter2D(im7, cv2.CV_32F, sobel)
[H, W] = np.shape(im7)
padded = np.pad(im7, pad_width=1, mode="constant", constant_values=0)
filtered = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float32)
for i in range(H):
    for j in range(W):
        region = padded[i : i + 3, j : j + 3]
        filtered[i, j] = np.sum(region * sobel)
sobel2 = np.array([[1,0,-1]], dtype=np.float32)
sobel1 = np.array([[1], [2], [1]], dtype=np.float32)
filtered2 = cv2.filter2D(cv2.filter2D(im7, cv2.CV_32F, sobel1),cv2.CV_32F,sobel2)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(6.5, 2.0))
ax[0].imshow(filtered1, cmap='gray')
ax[0].set_title('Sobel X Filter2D (a)')
ax[0].axis("off")
ax[1].imshow(filtered, cmap='gray')
ax[1].set_title('Sobel X Direct Method (b)')
ax[1].axis("off")
ax[2].imshow(filtered2, cmap='gray')
ax[2].set_title('Sobel X Separable Filter2D (c)')
ax[2].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

There is no visually noticeable difference between the SobelX filtering methods, but method (c), involving the decomposition of Sobel Horizontal into two vectors will have significantly reduced number of computations needed for the filtering output. Note that I padded the image when performing the direct filtering approach to avoid any errors or artifacts.

def zoomNN(img, scale):
        return cv2.resize(img, None, fx=scale, fy=scale, interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)
def zoomBilinear(img, scale):
        return cv2.resize(img, None, fx=scale, fy=scale, interpolation=cv2.INTER_LINEAR)
def ssd(img1, img2):
    diff = img1.astype(np.float32) - img2.astype(np.float32)
    return np.mean(diff ** 2)

im8_1_zoomed_nn = zoomNN(im8_1_small, scale=4)
im8_1_zoomed_bilinear = zoomBilinear(im8_1_small, scale=4)

bilinear_SSD1 = ssd(im8_1_big, im8_1_zoomed_bilinear)

print('Normalized SSD for Bilinear of Image 1: ', bilinear_SSD1)

im9 = cv2.imread("Images/flower.jpeg")
assert im9 is not None

im9_rgb = cv2.cvtColor(im9, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
H, W = im9.shape[:2]
mask = np.zeros((H, W), np.uint8)
bgdModel = np.zeros((1, 65), np.float64)
fgdModel = np.zeros((1, 65), np.float64)
rect = (10, 150, 550, 500)
cv2.grabCut(im9, mask, rect, bgdModel, fgdModel, iterCount=5, mode=cv2.GC_INIT_WITH_RECT)
fg_mask = np.where((mask == cv2.GC_FGD) | (mask == cv2.GC_PR_FGD), 255, 0).astype(np.uint8)
bg_mask = cv2.bitwise_not(fg_mask)
foreground = cv2.bitwise_and(im9_rgb, im9_rgb, mask=fg_mask)
background = cv2.bitwise_and(im9_rgb, im9_rgb, mask=bg_mask)
blurred_bg = cv2.GaussianBlur(background, (51, 51), sigmaX=0)
enhanced_image = cv2.add(foreground, blurred_bg)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(15, 5))
axes[0].imshow(im9_rgb)
axes[0].set_title("Original Image")
axes[0].axis("off")
axes[1].imshow(fg_mask, cmap="gray")
axes[1].set_title("Final Segmentation Mask")
axes[1].axis("off")
axes[2].imshow(foreground)
axes[2].set_title("Foreground Image")
axes[2].axis("off")
axes[3].imshow(background)
axes[3].set_title("Background Image")
axes[3].axis("off")
axes[4].imshow(enhanced_image)
axes[4].set_title("Enhanced Image (Blurred Background)")
axes[4].axis("off")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

For the GrabCut algorithm, I manually adjusted the region for the flower using the defined rect region (I wanted to select only the main flower and exclude the flower bud at the bottom of the image). When we blur the background, the region without the foreground is pure black pixels. These will get blurred with the surrounding regions, cause the dark edges present in the enhanced image.

def bilateral_filter_manual(image, radius, sigma_s, sigma_r):
    img = image.astype(np.float64)
    H, W = img.shape
    filtered = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.float64)
    for y in range(H):
        for x in range(W):
            I_x = img[y, x]
            weight_sum = 0.0
            pixel_acc = 0.0
            for dy in range(-radius, radius + 1):
                for dx in range(-radius, radius + 1):
                    yi = y + dy
                    xi = x + dx
                    if 0 <= yi < H and 0 <= xi < W:
                        I_xi = img[yi, xi]
                        spatial_dist_sq = dx * dx + dy * dy
                        g_s = math.exp(-spatial_dist_sq / (2.0 * sigma_s * sigma_s))
                        range_dist_sq = (I_xi - I_x) ** 2
                        g_r = math.exp(-range_dist_sq / (2.0 * sigma_r * sigma_r))
                        w = g_s * g_r
                        weight_sum += w
                        pixel_acc += w * I_xi
            filtered[y, x] = pixel_acc / weight_sum if weight_sum > 0 else I_x
    return np.clip(np.round(filtered), 0, 255).astype(np.uint8)

im10_r = im10_rgb[:, :, 0]
im10_r_bilateral = bilateral_filter_manual(im10_r, radius=7, sigma_s=75, sigma_r=75)
im10_g = im10_rgb[:, :, 1]
im10_g_bilateral = bilateral_filter_manual(im10_g, radius=7, sigma_s=75, sigma_r=75)
im10_b = im10_rgb[:, :, 2]
im10_b_bilateral = bilateral_filter_manual(im10_b, radius=7, sigma_s=75, sigma_r=75)

Normalized SSD between OpenCV2 Bilateral Filter and Manually Calculated Bilateral Filter:  201.461

I decided to the use the Sum of Squared Difference formula from the earlier questions to compare the efficacy of the Manual implementation and Direct implementation of Bilateral filtering (done on all three channels). Evidently, even with the same parameters, the manual calculation is not as good at filtering as the OpenCV2 function. I believe this is due to the fact that I am calculating the filter channelwise and combining, whereas the OpenCV2 function directly computes the joint distances on all channels together at once.
